about: The kinds of human situation a reading can be about, the same list for every language. A plan names one type for each part of each reading (parts[].type). A type is a guide to the feel of a reading, not a rule: each language tells its own country's instance, and a plan may pick a different type at the same point when its culture has a better fit with a similar feel, saying why in one line (type_note). A type is separate from a part's kind (story, article, exposition, learning-alongside): one type can be told as any kind. The examples are illustrations only, never texts to translate or adapt.

types.name: Meeting people
types.situation: Someone says who they are and introduces the people, animals and things around them.
types.practises: introducing and describing; the present of to be and to have; likes, numbers and colours
examples: A student in Seville introduces her flatmates and their cat.
A boy in Osaka introduces his family before dinner.

types.name: A day in a life
types.situation: Someone tells one ordinary day, from waking up to going to bed, and one thing that made it different.
types.practises: time and sequence (first, then, after); daily routine; telling a day in the present or the past
examples: A nurse in Lisbon works a night shift.
A schoolgirl in Seoul gets through the day of an exam.

types.name: Making plans
types.situation: Friends or a family plan an outing or a trip and settle when, where, how and who pays.
types.practises: inviting, accepting and refusing; the near future; can, must and want; questions
examples: Two friends in Berlin plan a Saturday at the lake.
A family in Mexico City plans a weekend on the coast.

types.name: A trip away
types.situation: A group or a family goes away for a few days: getting there, what they see, what goes wrong and what they bring home.
types.practises: transport and directions; places; telling events in the past; describing
examples: A school class spends a week on a farm in the Swedish countryside.
Cousins take the night train from Milan to Sicily.

types.name: A new place
types.situation: Someone moves somewhere new, finds their way and makes a first friend.
types.practises: describing a place; asking for and giving help; comparing here and there; who and where in relative clauses
examples: A girl moves from Porto to Lisbon and starts at a new school.
A young engineer moves from Hokkaido to Osaka for her first job.

types.name: At work
types.situation: Someone learns a job, gets through a working day or handles a client, a team or a deadline.
types.practises: requests and polite forms; instructions; the phone; reporting what was done
examples: A teenager works a first summer job at a pizzeria in Naples.
A junior architect in Copenhagen meets her first client.

types.name: A family celebration
types.situation: A family prepares for a big day, something goes wrong, and the day happens anyway.
types.practises: preparations and the future; wishes and toasts; telling the day in the past; family words
examples: A grandmother turns ninety in a village in Bavaria.
Two families meet for a wedding in Kraków.

types.name: A national celebration
types.situation: The whole country or a whole town marks a day of the year, and the people in the story spend it together.
types.practises: customs in the general present; dates and times; telling one evening from several points of view
examples: The Day of the Dead in Oaxaca.
Midsummer Eve on a Swedish island.
Lunar New Year in Taipei.

types.name: An emergency
types.situation: Something goes wrong fast, and people act, call for help and get through it.
types.practises: urgent instructions and the imperative; phone calls; what must be done; telling events hour by hour
examples: A pipe bursts at midnight in a flat in Madrid.
A hiker twists an ankle in the Scottish Highlands.

types.name: A mystery
types.situation: Something strange happens or goes missing, someone asks questions, and the answer surprises everyone.
types.practises: asking questions; describing people and things; the past with background and events; guessing (maybe, must have)
examples: A painting vanishes from a small museum in Kraków.
Footsteps sound in an empty house in a Kyoto alley.

types.name: A friendship
types.situation: Two people who seem to have nothing in common become friends, and each changes the other.
types.practises: character and feelings; telling a life; advice; regret and the past conditional
examples: A teenager in Athens and the old man who mends shoes downstairs.
A newcomer and a retired farmer in a Dutch village.

types.name: Asking why
types.situation: Someone who does not know, a child or a newcomer, asks why things are as they are, and someone who knows explains.
types.practises: why and because; explaining how things work; questions of every kind
examples: A girl in Norway asks her grandfather why the sun does not set in summer.
A boy in Cairo asks his aunt why the Nile once flooded every year.

types.name: Choosing a life
types.situation: Someone weighs the life they have against the one they want: a dream for later, or a working life looked back on.
types.practises: wishes and the subjunctive; hypotheses with if; the conditional; telling a life in the past
examples: A bank clerk in Warsaw dreams of opening a bakery.
A football coach in Porto Alegre looks back on forty years at one club.

types.name: Getting things sorted
types.situation: Someone deals with an office, a firm or a landlord, by letter or at a desk, and gets what they are owed.
types.practises: formal register and the set phrases of letters; complaining and claiming; explaining what happened; polite insistence
examples: A student in Rome renews her residence permit.
A tenant in Hamburg gets his deposit back.

types.name: A debate
types.situation: Two sides argue a question that matters to a town or a country; each admits a point, and someone decides.
types.practises: giving an opinion; agreeing and disagreeing; conceding (although, even if); the connectors of an argument
examples: A radio debate in Barcelona on holiday flats.
Parents in Seoul argue over Saturday classes.

types.name: A big question
types.situation: A short essay on a question people ask everywhere: what learning is, what makes a good life, what we owe each other.
types.practises: abstract nouns; defining and generalising; cause and consequence; the impersonal (one, people)
examples: What makes a good teacher? An essay for a Polish school magazine.
Why keep a promise? A short essay in the manner of the Confucian classics.

types.name: What the country is known for
types.situation: Something the country is famous for, and proud of, explained: where it comes from, who made it, and what it means to people there today.
types.practises: explaining and defining; the past for origins; the passive; opinions about it
examples: German engineering and the Mittelstand workshop.
Italian food and the Sunday meal.
Japanese craft and the master who trains an apprentice.

types.name: How people live
types.situation: A custom, a habit or a way of life of the country: what people do, why they do it, and what is changing.
types.practises: the general present; frequency; what is usual; comparing then and now
examples: Why Spaniards eat dinner at ten.
The Swedish coffee break, fika.
Shoes off at the door in Korea.

types.name: A moment in history
types.situation: A real moment of the country's past, told through the people who lived it or the place that keeps it.
types.practises: the narrative past; dates and centuries; the passive; reported speech
examples: The night the Berlin Wall opened.
The cave of Altamira and the paintings found there.
A day on the building site of the Great Wall at Shanhaiguan.

types.name: Cultures meet
types.situation: Two peoples meet, clash and mix, in a real historical moment or through people today who carry that history.
types.practises: comparison and contrast (while, whereas); the narrative past; cause and consequence; two points of view
examples: Christians, Muslims and Jews in Moorish Córdoba.
The Sami and the Swedish settlers in the far north.
Traders from four empires in the market of Kashgar on the Silk Road.

types.name: How others see us
types.situation: How outsiders picture the country, what they get wrong, and what the people who live there make of it.
types.practises: reported opinion; clichés and what lies behind them; concession; humour and irony
examples: What Italians make of Hollywood's Tuscany.
Tokyo residents read a foreign guidebook to their city.

types.name: A place portrait
types.situation: A town, a region or a landmark: what it looks like, what people do there, and why it matters to the country.
types.practises: describing places; there is and there are; location; a few dates of history
examples: The canals of Amsterdam.
The market square of Kraków.
The cave town of Matera.

written.about: The type of each reading a language's course has already written, recorded here because written modules are not edited to carry one. The plan's readings carry their own type.
